mistakes.title: Subnetting: forgetting the −2 or the wrong octet
mistakes.wrong: Usable hosts equal the total number of addresses, and the block size applies to the 4th octet for every prefix.
mistakes.right: Usable hosts = 2^h − 2 (except /31 and /32). The block size applies to the 'interesting' octet — the 3rd octet for /17–/24, the 2nd for /9–/16.
mistakes.recognize: Answer options include both 2^h and 2^h − 2 (e.g., 32 and 30), or the prefix is shorter than /24.
mistakes.avoid: Write h and the interesting octet before calculating. Check: does your answer subtract the network and broadcast?
mistakes.example: 10.1.0.0/21 → interesting octet 3, block 8 → 10.1.0.0–10.1.7.255, 2,046 usable hosts (not 2,048, and not a /24-style answer).

mistakes.title: Confusing network and broadcast addresses
mistakes.wrong: x.x.x.0 is always the network address and x.x.x.255 is always the broadcast.
mistakes.right: Network = all host bits 0; broadcast = all host bits 1, for that prefix. In a /22, 10.1.5.255 can be a valid host and 10.1.7.255 is the broadcast.
mistakes.recognize: The question asks for 'first usable', 'last usable', or 'valid host' with a prefix shorter than /24.
mistakes.avoid: Always derive network and broadcast from the block, never from the last octet alone.

mistakes.title: Confusing VLANs and subnets
mistakes.wrong: Putting two hosts in the same VLAN lets them talk even if their IP subnets differ, or a VLAN routes traffic by itself.
mistakes.right: A VLAN is a Layer 2 broadcast domain; a subnet is a Layer 3 address range. Normally one VLAN = one subnet, and inter-VLAN traffic needs a router or Layer 3 switch.
mistakes.recognize: A host can reach nothing outside its VLAN, or a host is in the right VLAN but has an address from another VLAN's subnet.
mistakes.avoid: Check both: the switch port VLAN (show vlan brief) and the host IP/mask/gateway.
mistakes.example: PC in VLAN 20 configured with 192.168.10.50/24 (VLAN 10's subnet) cannot reach its gateway.

mistakes.title: Misunderstanding trunk ports
mistakes.wrong: A trunk automatically carries every VLAN, and the native VLAN is tagged like the others.
mistakes.right: Trunks carry only VLANs that are allowed AND exist on the switch; the native VLAN is untagged and must match on both ends. 'allowed vlan X' without 'add' replaces the list.
mistakes.recognize: show interfaces trunk output, native VLAN mismatch messages, or an 'allowed vlan' command without 'add'.
mistakes.avoid: Read all three trunk lists (allowed, active, forwarding) and check the native VLAN on both ends.
mistakes.example: switchport trunk allowed vlan 40 on a trunk carrying 10,20,30 leaves only VLAN 40.

mistakes.title: Misunderstanding STP
mistakes.wrong: The switch with the highest priority or most connections becomes root; the root bridge has a root port.
mistakes.right: Lowest bridge ID (priority, then MAC) wins. The root bridge has no root port — all its ports are designated. Path selection uses total cost, not hop count.
mistakes.recognize: Questions giving priorities and MACs, or asking which port blocks.
mistakes.avoid: Follow the order: root bridge → root ports → designated ports → everything else discards.
mistakes.example: Priorities 4096 vs 32768: the 4096 switch is root even if its MAC is higher.

mistakes.title: Confusing administrative distance and metric
mistakes.wrong: The route with the lowest metric always wins, or AD is compared between routes to different prefixes.
mistakes.right: Order: longest prefix → lowest AD (between different sources for the same prefix) → lowest metric (within the same protocol).
mistakes.recognize: Routes from different protocols in the table, or [AD/metric] values in brackets.
mistakes.avoid: First filter by prefix length; only then look at AD; only then at metric.

mistakes.title: Misreading routing tables
mistakes.wrong: The first matching line in the output is used, or 'L' means loopback.
mistakes.right: IOS uses the longest matching prefix wherever it appears. L = local /32 for the router's own interface IP; C = connected subnet; S* = static default.
mistakes.recognize: An exhibit with overlapping routes like /16, /22 and /24.
mistakes.avoid: Write the destination, list every matching prefix, pick the longest, then read next hop and exit interface on that line.

mistakes.title: Confusing wildcard masks and subnet masks
mistakes.wrong: ACLs and OSPF network statements use subnet masks, or the wildcard is just the mask reversed in order.
mistakes.right: Wildcard = 255.255.255.255 − subnet mask; 0 bits must match, 1 bits are ignored. /26 → 0.0.0.63.
mistakes.recognize: Options containing both 255.255.255.192 and 0.0.0.63 for an ACL or OSPF command.
mistakes.avoid: In ACLs and 'network … area' commands, expect small numbers at the end (0.0.0.x).

mistakes.title: Misunderstanding ACL processing
mistakes.wrong: The most specific entry wins, or traffic not denied is permitted.
mistakes.right: Entries are processed top-down; the first match decides; anything unmatched is dropped by the implicit deny.
mistakes.recognize: An ACL with a broad permit above a specific deny, or an ACL with only deny lines.
mistakes.avoid: Walk the packet line by line and stop at the first match; remember the invisible deny at the end.
mistakes.example: permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 then deny host 192.168.1.66 → .66 is permitted.

mistakes.title: Confusing TCP and UDP
mistakes.wrong: Anything important uses TCP; DNS is UDP-only; TFTP is TCP like FTP.
mistakes.right: Choice depends on needs: reliability → TCP; low overhead/real time → UDP. DNS uses both; TFTP is UDP 69; TACACS+ is TCP 49; RADIUS is UDP.
mistakes.recognize: Port/transport matching questions and 'which uses a handshake' questions.
mistakes.avoid: Memorize the exceptions list: DNS (both), TFTP (UDP), TACACS+ (TCP), Syslog (UDP).
mistakes.example: SNMP is important but uses UDP 161/162.

mistakes.title: Misunderstanding IPv6 address types
mistakes.wrong: FE80 addresses are routable, IPv6 uses broadcast, or FD00 addresses are global.
mistakes.right: Link-local FE80::/10 never leaves the link; IPv6 has no broadcast (multicast FF00::/8 instead); FC00::/7 (FD..) is unique local; 2000::/3 is global unicast.
mistakes.recognize: Questions asking which address a router uses as a next hop, or which address type a prefix is.
mistakes.avoid: Classify by the first hex digits: 2/3 global, FD unique local, FE80 link-local, FF multicast.
mistakes.example: OSPFv3 neighbors use link-local addresses as next hops.

mistakes.title: Confusing DHCP and DNS
mistakes.wrong: DNS assigns IP addresses, or DHCP resolves names.
mistakes.right: DHCP gives a host its IP settings (address, mask, gateway, DNS server). DNS translates names to addresses.
mistakes.recognize: Symptoms: 169.254.x.x address → DHCP problem; can ping IPs but not names → DNS problem.
mistakes.avoid: Ask: is the host missing its own address (DHCP) or failing to resolve names (DNS)?
mistakes.example: ping 8.8.8.8 works, ping www.cisco.com fails → check DNS, not DHCP.

mistakes.title: Confusing NAT and PAT
mistakes.wrong: Dynamic NAT lets unlimited hosts share a pool, or inside global means the private address.
mistakes.right: Dynamic NAT is one public address per active host; PAT ('overload') shares an address using ports. Inside local = private inside address; inside global = its public translation.
mistakes.recognize: Translation tables with ports, pool exhaustion scenarios, and NAT terminology questions.
mistakes.avoid: Look for the 'overload' keyword and port numbers in the translation table.
mistakes.example: ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB (no overload) fails once all pool addresses are in use.

glossary.simple: The VLAN tagging standard.
glossary.technical: Inserts a 4-byte tag (TPID 0x8100, PCP, DEI, 12-bit VLAN ID) between source MAC and EtherType.

glossary.simple: Port-based network access control.
glossary.technical: Supplicant, authenticator (switch/AP/WLC), authentication server (RADIUS); uses EAP. Basis of WPA-Enterprise.

glossary.simple: Controls who can log in, what they can do, and records what they did.
glossary.technical: Framework enabled with 'aaa new-model'; uses local users or RADIUS/TACACS+ servers through method lists evaluated left to right.

glossary.simple: An ordered list of permit/deny rules.
glossary.technical: Processed top-down with first-match and an implicit deny. Standard ACLs match source only; extended ACLs match protocol, addresses and ports. Applied with ip access-group (interfaces) or access-class (VTY).

glossary.simple: How much a router trusts a route source.
glossary.technical: Compared only between routes to the same prefix; lower wins. Connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200.

glossary.simple: Agentless configuration management tool.
glossary.technical: Push model over SSH/APIs; YAML playbooks; inventory and modules; written in Python.

glossary.simple: One address shared by several devices; the nearest one answers.
glossary.technical: An IPv6 unicast address assigned to multiple interfaces; routing delivers packets to the topologically closest.

glossary.simple: A defined way for software to talk to other software.
glossary.technical: Controllers expose northbound REST APIs to applications and use southbound interfaces to configure devices.

glossary.simple: The 169.254.x.x address a host gives itself when DHCP fails.
glossary.technical: IPv4 link-local range 169.254.0.0/16; signals that no DHCP server responded.

glossary.simple: Finds the MAC address that belongs to an IPv4 address.
glossary.technical: Broadcast request, unicast reply; results cached in the ARP table. Hosts ARP for the default gateway when the destination is remote.

glossary.simple: A standalone access point configured on its own.
glossary.technical: Handles all 802.11 functions locally; no WLC required.

glossary.simple: A network under one administrative routing policy.
glossary.technical: Identified by an AS number; BGP routes between autonomous systems, IGPs route within one.

glossary.simple: The OSPF router ready to replace the DR.
glossary.technical: Elected on broadcast networks by second-highest priority/RID; forms full adjacencies with all routers.

glossary.simple: The routing protocol of the internet.
glossary.technical: Path-vector EGP over TCP 179; AD 20 for eBGP and 200 for iBGP.

glossary.simple: Spanning tree control message.
glossary.technical: Carries bridge ID, root bridge ID and path cost; root sends hellos every 2 s by default.

glossary.simple: Shuts down an edge port if a switch is connected.
glossary.technical: Err-disables a PortFast port that receives any BPDU. Recover with shutdown/no shutdown or errdisable recovery.

glossary.simple: The identity used in the STP root election.
glossary.technical: Priority (default 32768, multiples of 4096) + VLAN system ID extension + MAC address; lowest wins.

glossary.simple: All devices that receive each other's broadcasts.
glossary.technical: Bounded by routers and VLANs; each VLAN is one broadcast domain.

glossary.full: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points
glossary.simple: Tunnel between lightweight APs and a WLC.
glossary.technical: UDP 5246 control (DTLS-encrypted) and UDP 5247 data.

glossary.simple: Cisco's enterprise network controller (formerly DNA Center).
glossary.technical: Provides automation, assurance and policy; exposes northbound REST APIs.

glossary.simple: Shows which Cisco devices are directly connected.
glossary.technical: Cisco-proprietary Layer 2 protocol; 60 s timer, 180 s holdtime. show cdp neighbors [detail].

glossary.simple: Writing a mask as a prefix length like /24.
glossary.technical: Removes classful boundaries and allows summarization and VLSM.

glossary.simple: A segment where simultaneous transmissions can collide.
glossary.technical: Each switch port is its own collision domain; full duplex eliminates collisions.

glossary.simple: A lightweight package that runs an app on a shared OS kernel.
glossary.technical: Packages the application and dependencies; shares the host kernel, unlike a VM.

glossary.simple: The part of a device that decides how to forward.
glossary.technical: Routing protocols, STP, ARP — they build the tables used by the data plane.

glossary.simple: Central software that manages many network devices.
glossary.technical: Holds policy and automation logic; examples include Catalyst Center and WLCs; uses northbound and southbound interfaces.

glossary.simple: A 3-bit Layer 2 priority marking.
glossary.technical: Carried in the PCP field of the 802.1Q tag (values 0–7).

glossary.simple: Error check that detects corrupted frames.
glossary.technical: Stored in the Ethernet FCS; CRC errors suggest cabling problems, interference or duplex mismatch.

glossary.simple: The four basic data operations.
glossary.technical: Map to HTTP POST, GET, PUT/PATCH and DELETE in REST APIs.

glossary.full: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance
glossary.simple: How Wi-Fi devices take turns.
glossary.technical: Stations listen, wait a random backoff and use acknowledgments because they cannot detect collisions while transmitting.

glossary.full: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection
glossary.simple: How old shared Ethernet handled collisions.
glossary.technical: Half-duplex method: detect collision, send jam signal, back off. Not used on full-duplex links.

glossary.simple: Blocks fake ARP messages.
glossary.technical: Validates ARP on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table (or ARP ACLs); default limit 15 pps on untrusted ports.

glossary.simple: The part of a device that forwards traffic.
glossary.technical: Frame switching, routing lookups, ACL filtering, NAT — performed on user traffic.

glossary.simple: The router a host uses to reach other networks.
glossary.technical: Must be in the host's own subnet; hosts ARP for it when the destination is remote.

glossary.simple: The route used when nothing more specific matches.
glossary.technical: 0.0.0.0/0 (IPv4) or ::/0 (IPv6); shown as S* and 'Gateway of last resort'.

glossary.simple: Automatically gives devices their IP settings.
glossary.technical: DORA exchange; server UDP 67, client UDP 68; relayed across subnets with ip helper-address.

glossary.simple: Forwards DHCP requests to a server on another subnet.
glossary.technical: ip helper-address on the client-facing interface converts broadcasts to unicast and sets giaddr.

glossary.simple: Stops rogue DHCP servers on a switch.
glossary.technical: Untrusted ports drop DHCP server messages; builds a binding table of MAC, IP, VLAN and port.

glossary.simple: Translates names into IP addresses.
glossary.technical: UDP 53 for queries, TCP 53 for zone transfers/large responses. Records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, NS.

glossary.simple: The OSPF router that coordinates updates on a shared segment.
glossary.technical: Elected on broadcast networks by highest priority then router ID; non-preemptive; reached at 224.0.0.6.

glossary.simple: A 6-bit Layer 3 QoS marking.
glossary.technical: In the IP header's DS field (0–63). Voice is typically EF (46).

glossary.simple: Cisco protocol that negotiates trunk links.
glossary.technical: Modes dynamic auto / dynamic desirable; auto + auto = access. Disable with switchport nonegotiate.

glossary.simple: Whether a link can send and receive at the same time.
glossary.technical: Half duplex uses CSMA/CD; full duplex sends and receives simultaneously. A mismatch causes late collisions and CRC errors.

glossary.simple: Bundles several links into one logical link.
glossary.technical: Negotiated with LACP (active/passive) or PAgP (desirable/auto), or static 'on'; per-flow load balancing.

glossary.simple: Builds an IPv6 interface ID from a MAC address.
glossary.technical: Split the MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit of the first byte.

glossary.simple: The error-check trailer of an Ethernet frame.
glossary.technical: 4-byte CRC; receivers discard frames whose FCS does not match.

glossary.simple: Keeps the default gateway available if a router fails.
glossary.technical: Routers share a virtual IP/MAC: HSRP and GLBP (Cisco), VRRP (standard).

glossary.simple: AP mode for branches that can switch traffic locally.
glossary.technical: Control goes to the WLC; client data can be switched locally, and the AP keeps serving clients if the WAN fails.

glossary.simple: A backup static route.
glossary.technical: Configured with an AD higher than the primary route so it is installed only when the primary disappears.

glossary.simple: Cisco FHRP that load-balances gateways.
glossary.technical: An AVG answers ARP with different virtual MACs so several AVFs forward at once.

glossary.simple: Cisco FHRP with active and standby routers.
glossary.technical: Default priority 100, preemption disabled by default; v1 virtual MAC 0000.0C07.ACxx.

glossary.simple: The number a web server returns to describe the result.
glossary.technical: 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404), 5xx server error (500).

glossary.simple: Software that runs virtual machines.
glossary.technical: Type 1 runs on bare metal (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM); Type 2 runs on a host OS.

glossary.simple: Renting compute, storage and networking from a provider.
glossary.technical: The customer manages OS and applications; compare PaaS and SaaS.

glossary.simple: Error and diagnostic messages for IP.
glossary.technical: Used by ping (echo request/reply) and traceroute; IP protocol 1. ICMPv6 also carries NDP.

glossary.simple: The invisible last line of every ACL.
glossary.technical: Denies anything not matched by an explicit entry.

glossary.simple: The public address that represents an inside host.
glossary.technical: Assigned by NAT/PAT; seen by hosts on the internet.

glossary.simple: The real address of an inside host.
glossary.technical: Usually an RFC 1918 private address before translation.

glossary.simple: Routing traffic between VLANs.
glossary.technical: Router-on-a-stick subinterfaces (encapsulation dot1Q) or Layer 3 switch SVIs.

glossary.simple: Inspects traffic inline and blocks attacks.
glossary.technical: An IDS only monitors and alerts; an IPS can drop malicious packets. Often integrated in NGFWs.

glossary.simple: Framework for encrypting IP traffic.
glossary.technical: Provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication and anti-replay; ESP (IP 50), AH (IP 51), IKE on UDP 500.

glossary.simple: 128-bit addressing for the modern internet.
glossary.technical: Hex hextets, no broadcast, NDP instead of ARP, SLAAC and link-local addresses on every interface.

glossary.simple: A simple text format for structured data.
glossary.technical: Objects {} with double-quoted keys, arrays [], values: string, number, boolean, null, object, array.

glossary.simple: Standard protocol for building EtherChannels.
glossary.technical: IEEE 802.3ad/802.1AX; modes active and passive; passive + passive does not form.

glossary.simple: An AP managed by a wireless LAN controller.
glossary.technical: Split-MAC: AP handles real-time 802.11 functions; WLC handles management, security and RF.

glossary.simple: An address valid only on the local link.
glossary.technical: IPv6 FE80::/10, created automatically; used for NDP and as routing next hops. IPv4 equivalent: 169.254.0.0/16.

glossary.simple: Vendor-neutral neighbor discovery.
glossary.technical: IEEE 802.1AB; 30 s timer, 120 s holdtime; enable with lldp run.

glossary.simple: The router picks the most specific matching route.
glossary.technical: Evaluated before administrative distance and metric.

glossary.simple: A piece of OSPF topology information.
glossary.technical: Stored in the LSDB; all routers in an area have identical LSDBs.

glossary.simple: The hardware address of a network interface.
glossary.technical: 48 bits; first 24 bits are the OUI; FFFF.FFFF.FFFF is broadcast.

glossary.simple: A switch's list of which MAC lives on which port.
glossary.technical: Learned from source MACs; dynamic entries age out after 300 s by default.

glossary.simple: How administrators operate a device.
glossary.technical: SSH, SNMP, Syslog, NTP, HTTPS management.

glossary.simple: A routing protocol's measure of path cost.
glossary.technical: Compares routes from the same protocol: OSPF cost, RIP hop count, EIGRP composite.

glossary.simple: Logging in with two or more kinds of proof.
glossary.technical: Combines factors from different categories: know, have, are.

glossary.simple: One-to-group delivery.
glossary.technical: IPv4 224.0.0.0/4; IPv6 FF00::/8 (FF02::1 all nodes, FF02::2 all routers).

glossary.simple: Changes IP addresses as traffic passes through a router.
glossary.technical: Usually private inside local to public inside global; static, dynamic pool, or PAT (overload).

glossary.simple: The VLAN sent without a tag on a trunk.
glossary.technical: Default VLAN 1; must match on both ends; best practice is an unused VLAN.

glossary.simple: IPv6's way of finding neighbors and routers.
glossary.technical: ICMPv6 RS 133, RA 134, NS 135, NA 136; replaces ARP and supports SLAAC.

glossary.simple: A protocol for configuring devices with structured data.
glossary.technical: Runs over SSH (TCP 830) using YANG data models; a southbound interface.

glossary.simple: A firewall that understands applications.
glossary.technical: Stateful filtering plus application visibility and control, IPS, URL filtering and anti-malware.

glossary.simple: How applications talk to a controller.
glossary.technical: Typically REST APIs with JSON.

glossary.simple: Keeps device clocks synchronized.
glossary.technical: UDP 123; stratum shows distance from the reference clock (lower is better).

glossary.simple: A link-state routing protocol.
glossary.technical: Floods LSAs, builds an LSDB, runs SPF; AD 110; metric cost; Hello 10/Dead 40 on broadcast; IP protocol 89.

glossary.simple: The vendor part of a MAC address.
glossary.technical: First 24 bits of the 48-bit MAC.

glossary.simple: Virtual networks built on top of the physical network.
glossary.technical: Tunnels such as VXLAN carry user traffic across the underlay.

glossary.simple: A provider runs the platform; you deploy code.
glossary.technical: Provider manages infrastructure, OS and runtime.

glossary.simple: Cisco protocol for building EtherChannels.
glossary.technical: Modes desirable and auto; auto + auto does not form.

glossary.simple: Many hosts share one public IP using port numbers.
glossary.technical: NAT overload; translations identified by IP + port.

glossary.simple: Powering devices through the network cable.
glossary.technical: 802.3af 15.4 W, 802.3at 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60/90 W at the PSE.

glossary.simple: Limits which MAC addresses may use a switch port.
glossary.technical: Default max 1 MAC, violation shutdown; modes protect, restrict, shutdown; sticky learning.

glossary.simple: Lets host ports start forwarding immediately.
glossary.technical: Skips listening/learning on edge ports; pair with BPDU Guard.

glossary.simple: The number of network bits in an address, written /n.
Prioritizes important traffic when links are busy.
glossary.technical: Classification, marking, queuing (CBWFQ/LLQ), congestion avoidance (WRED), policing and shaping.

glossary.simple: Standard AAA protocol for network access.
glossary.technical: UDP 1812/1813; encrypts only the password; combines authentication and authorization.

glossary.simple: A simple, stateless style of web API.
glossary.technical: HTTP methods on URIs; stateless, client-server, cacheable, uniform interface.

glossary.simple: REST-style access to YANG-modeled device data.
glossary.technical: Uses HTTPS with JSON or XML; a southbound interface.

glossary.simple: The center of the spanning tree.
glossary.technical: Switch with the lowest bridge ID; all its ports are designated.

glossary.simple: Prevents an unwanted switch from becoming root.
glossary.technical: Puts a port into root-inconsistent state if it receives superior BPDUs.

glossary.simple: The unique 32-bit name of an OSPF router.
glossary.technical: Manual router-id → highest loopback IP → highest active interface IP.

glossary.simple: The router's list of known networks and how to reach them.
glossary.technical: Entries show source code, prefix, [AD/metric], next hop and exit interface.

glossary.simple: Faster version of spanning tree.
glossary.technical: IEEE 802.1w; states discarding, learning, forwarding; roles root, designated, alternate, backup. Cisco's per-VLAN version is Rapid PVST+.

glossary.simple: Using a complete application delivered by a provider.
glossary.technical: The provider manages everything; the customer uses the app.

glossary.simple: WPA3-Personal's password-based key exchange.
glossary.technical: Resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy.

glossary.simple: Central software controls how the network behaves.
glossary.technical: Centralizes control/management logic on a controller with northbound and southbound interfaces; devices still forward traffic.

glossary.simple: IPv6 hosts build their own addresses.
glossary.technical: Prefix from Router Advertisements + interface ID (EUI-64 or random).

glossary.simple: Lets monitoring systems read and change device data.
glossary.technical: UDP 161 polls, UDP 162 traps/informs; MIBs and OIDs; v3 adds authentication and encryption.

glossary.simple: How a controller talks to network devices.
glossary.technical: NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH/CLI, SNMP.

glossary.simple: The algorithm OSPF uses to compute routes.
glossary.technical: Dijkstra's algorithm run on the LSDB by each router.

glossary.simple: Data center topology where each leaf connects to every spine.
glossary.technical: Predictable leaf–spine–leaf paths for east-west traffic; no leaf-leaf or spine-spine links.

glossary.simple: Encrypted remote command-line access.
glossary.technical: TCP 22; requires hostname, domain name, RSA keys and VTY 'transport input ssh'.

glossary.simple: The name of a wireless network.
glossary.technical: Advertised in beacons; several APs sharing an SSID form an ESS. BSSID is the AP radio's MAC.

glossary.simple: A manually configured route.
glossary.technical: ip route / ipv6 route; default AD 1; installed only when the next hop is reachable.

glossary.simple: Prevents Layer 2 loops.
glossary.technical: Elects a root bridge and blocks redundant ports; 802.1D costs 100/19/4/2 for 10M/100M/1G/10G.

glossary.simple: Shows which part of an IP address is the network.
glossary.technical: Contiguous 1 bits for the network portion; valid octets 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255.

glossary.simple: A routed interface for a VLAN on a switch.
glossary.technical: interface vlan X; up/up only if the VLAN exists with an active port; requires ip routing to route.

glossary.simple: Connects devices within a LAN and forwards frames by MAC address.
glossary.technical: Learns source MACs, forwards known unicasts, floods broadcasts and unknown unicasts within the VLAN; each port is a collision domain.

glossary.simple: Standard for sending log messages.
glossary.technical: UDP 514; severities 0 Emergency … 7 Debugging; a configured level includes all more severe levels.

glossary.full: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
glossary.simple: Cisco-developed AAA protocol for device administration.
glossary.technical: TCP 49; encrypts the whole payload; separates authentication, authorization and accounting.

glossary.simple: Reliable, connection-oriented transport.
glossary.technical: Three-way handshake, sequencing, acknowledgments, windowing; 20-byte minimum header.

glossary.simple: Unencrypted remote command-line access.
glossary.technical: TCP 23; sends credentials in clear text — use SSH instead.

glossary.simple: Infrastructure-as-code tool using declarative files.
glossary.technical: HCL language, providers, plan/apply workflow and a state file.

glossary.simple: Simple file transfer without login.
glossary.technical: UDP 69; no authentication or encryption; used for IOS images and configs on trusted networks.

glossary.simple: A link that carries multiple VLANs.
glossary.technical: 802.1Q tags every VLAN except the native VLAN; verify with show interfaces trunk.

glossary.simple: Lightweight, connectionless transport.
glossary.technical: No handshake, acknowledgments or ordering; 8-byte header. Used by DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, voice.

glossary.simple: The physical network under a fabric.
glossary.technical: Provides IP reachability for overlay tunnels (IS-IS in SD-Access).

glossary.simple: A complete computer running in software.
glossary.technical: Runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor.

glossary.simple: A separate logical network on a switch.
glossary.technical: A Layer 2 broadcast domain; normal 1–1005, extended 1006–4094; usually maps to one subnet.

glossary.simple: Using different subnet sizes in one address block.
glossary.technical: Allocate largest subnets first on correct boundaries to avoid overlap.

glossary.simple: An encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network.
glossary.technical: Site-to-site (gateway to gateway) or remote access (client to gateway); often IPsec or TLS.

glossary.simple: Several separate routing tables in one router.
glossary.technical: Allows overlapping address space; VRF-lite without MPLS.

glossary.simple: Standards-based FHRP.
glossary.technical: Master/backup routers; preemption enabled by default; virtual MAC 0000.5E00.01xx.

glossary.simple: A tunneling format for overlay networks.
glossary.technical: MAC-in-UDP encapsulation with a 24-bit VNI; the SD-Access data plane.

glossary.simple: An inverse mask used in ACLs and OSPF.
glossary.technical: 0 bits must match, 1 bits are ignored; 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask for a contiguous block.

glossary.simple: Centrally manages lightweight access points.
glossary.technical: Uses CAPWAP; maps WLANs to interfaces/VLANs; AireOS LAG requires a static EtherChannel.

glossary.simple: Common Wi-Fi security standard.
glossary.technical: AES-CCMP encryption; Personal (PSK) or Enterprise (802.1X).

glossary.simple: Current Wi-Fi security standard.
glossary.technical: SAE for Personal, mandatory Protected Management Frames, 192-bit option for Enterprise.

glossary.simple: Human-readable data format that uses indentation.
glossary.technical: Used for Ansible playbooks; indentation defines structure.
